lessons.title: Java Stream Pipeline Basics
lessons.summary: Explain source, intermediate operations and terminal operations with a small Java example.

provenance.sourceDescription: JIA editorial starter content; authored for the academy and reviewed for Java 17 syntax.

blocks.title: Overview
blocks.body: A Stream describes a computation over a data source; it does not store the elements or mutate the source by default.

blocks.title: Concise interview answer
body: A stream pipeline has a source, zero or more intermediate operations, and one terminal operation.
Intermediate operations are lazy; traversal begins when a terminal operation executes.
A stream is single-use, and side effects should be avoided in behavioral parameters.

blocks.title: Filter and map
blocks.source:
List<String> names = List.of("Ada", "Ben", "Asha");
List<String> result = names.stream()
    .filter(name -> name.startsWith("A"))
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .toList(); // [ADA, ASHA]
blocks.explanation: filter retains matching elements, map transforms each retained element, and toList is the terminal operation.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body: Do not reuse a consumed stream. Do not expect intermediate operations to run without a terminal operation. Avoid modifying shared state from stream lambdas.

blocks.title: Follow-up questions
blocks.body: How does map differ from flatMap? When is parallelStream unsuitable? What guarantees does Stream.toList provide?

lessons.title: The equals and hashCode Contract
lessons.summary: Understand equality semantics and hash-based collection correctness.

provenance.sourceDescription: JIA editorial starter content; original explanatory material with a Java 17 example.

blocks.title: Overview
blocks.body: Logical equality is defined by equals. hashCode supports bucket selection in hash-based collections.

blocks.title: Concise interview answer
body: If two objects are equal according to equals, they must return the same hashCode.
Unequal objects may share a hash code; collisions are permitted.
Fields used by equality should not change while an object is used as a hash-map key.

blocks.title: Value object example
blocks.explanation: A record derives equals and hashCode from its components; use explicit implementations for classes with custom equality.

blocks.title: Collection impact
blocks.body: A HashMap first uses the hash code to locate a bucket and then equality to identify a matching key. Violating the contract can make logically equivalent lookups fail.

prompt.text: When does a Java Stream pipeline normally begin traversing its source?

questions.explanation: Intermediate operations are lazy; a terminal operation triggers evaluation of the pipeline.

provenance.sourceDescription: JIA original assessment question aligned to the stream-pipeline lesson.

prompt.text: If two Java objects are equal according to equals, they must have the same hashCode.

questions.explanation: The equals/hashCode contract requires equal objects to have equal hash codes; the reverse is not required.
